query: Earlier studies established BCC refractory high-entropy alloys such as MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW with excellent high-temperature mechanical properties, while systems including AlNbTiV, NbHfTiV, and AlCrNbTiV also showed favorable mechanical behavior. NbZrTi-based alloys provide broad scope for regulating composition and properties, but changes in elemental identity and proportion can alter both phase constitution and mechanical performance. Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered BCC solid solution with a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa; however, its high Mo content increases the electronegativity difference and is associated with reduced plasticity. Given the constraint of preserving high strength while improving plasticity under room-temperature compression, what single intervention could overcome this limitation? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and its mechanism, predicts quantitative or directional changes relative to equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo, defines the conditions and limits of the effect, cites supporting evidence from the prior results summarized above, and proposes an experiment with explicit observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a deep cryogenic treatment (DCT) to equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo will improve its room-temperature plasticity without compromising its high compressive yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo, a disordered BCC solid solution with high Mo content, which exhibits a high compressive yield strength (~1719 MPa) but limited plasticity at room temperature due to the high electronegativity difference introduced by Mo.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to a deep cryogenic treatment (e.g., immersion in liquid nitrogen at approximately -196°C for an optimized dwell time) followed by a controlled warm-up cycle.
generation.conditions: The treatment is applied post-casting/heat treatment and prior to room-temperature mechanical testing. The alloy is then subjected to standard room-temperature compressive tests.
generation.structural_mediator: Modification of the microstructure through cryogenically induced phase transitions or refinement of dislocation structures, potentially increasing the number of active slip systems.
generation.mechanism: DCT may induce subtle phase transitions or relieve internal stresses related to the high Mo content, expanding the operational slip systems or reducing localized embrittlement. This microstructural refinement can enhance dislocation mobility leading to improved plasticity while preserving the high yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under room-temperature compression, DCT-treated samples will show a significant increase in plasticity (for example, a measurable increase in plastic strain, potentially on the order of 10–50% relative improvement) with yield strength maintained within about 5% of the untreated state.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo exhibiting a yield strength of approximately 1719 MPa but limited room-temperature plasticity.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected within an optimized range of DCT parameters (temperature, duration, and warming rate). Variations in these parameters may lead to insufficient microstructural modification or even adverse effects if the treatment is too severe.
generation.uncertainty: While similar alloys (e.g., HfNbTaTiZr) have shown improvements with DCT, the precise magnitude of plasticity enhancement and possible microstructural changes in NbZrTiHfMo are not yet fully characterized, given the potential influence of the high Mo content.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo samples from the same cast batch. Subject one set to a controlled deep cryogenic treatment (immersion in liquid nitrogen at −196°C for the predetermined time, followed by a standardized warm-up protocol) while keeping the other set as untreated controls. Subsequently perform room-temperature compressive testing on both sets and conduct microstructural characterization (using XRD, TEM) to detect any DCT-induced phase modifications.
measurements: Microstructural features including phase constitution and dislocation configurations via XRD and TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the DCT-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant (e.g., ≥10%) improvement in plastic strain without a reduction in yield strength beyond 5% compared to controls, or if no indicative microstructural changes are detected, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractHfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy has wide application prospects as a biomedical material, and the use of laser additive manufacturing can solve the forming problems faced by the alloy. In view of the characteristics of the one-time forming of additive manufacturing methods, it is necessary to develop non-mechanical processing modification methods. In this paper, deep cryogenic treatment (DCT) is first applied to the modification of a HEA with BCC structure, then the post-processing method of DCT is combined with laser melting deposition (LMD) technology to successfully realize the coordinated improvement of forming and strength–ductility synergistic improvement in lightweight Hf0.25NbTa0.25TiZr alloy. The final tensile strength of the alloy after DCT treatment is 25% higher than that of the as-cast alloy and 11% higher than that of the as-deposited alloy, and the elongation is increased by 48% and 10%, respectively. In addition, DCT also achieves induced phase transition without additional deformation.Keywords: laser melting deposition, high entropy alloy, deep cryogenic treatment, 3D printing, defects, strength–ductility synergistic improvement
